metadata.title: AI in essay-based assessment: Student adoption, usage, and performance

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study uses a single-institution undergraduate economics class (Australia) and merges a voluntary Qualtrics survey (n=69 respondents) with administrative records (final mark and prior performance). The paper does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures; therefore, no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is specified. Because the analysis is based on a convenience sample from one course rather than an international probability sample, standard ILSA-style weighting is not applicable. The main data preparation step is restricting to survey respondents and then running regression models with pre-semester GPA and earlier course test scores as controls to address ability confounding.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are course assessment marks (0–100) and criterion subscores, not ILSA-style cognitive achievement scales generated via PVs. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper focuses on regression analyses using the available survey respondents and does not describe any imputation or explicit exclusion rules for missing covariates/outcomes. Given the small analytic sample (69), the absence of a documented missing-data strategy limits transparency about potential bias from incomplete records.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were recruited from a single second-year undergraduate economics class at an Australian university. The analytic sample for the quantitative regression analyses is the subset of students who completed the post-assessment survey about AI tool use (69 respondents out of 187 in the class). The paper reports that survey respondents differed from non-respondents on GPA and full-time enrolment, and it controls for ability using pre-semester GPA and earlier course assessment scores; no additional grade-level or task-level filtering is described.

main_findings.dataset_used: Undergraduate economics research proposal (Australia, 2023 cohort; essay-based assessment)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regression (no ML). Used AI coefficient: Model (1) +5.391 (SE 4.323), p not significant; Models with controls (4–5) estimate effect less than 1 mark; R² ranges from 0.023 (unconditional) to 0.488 (Model 5).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using undergraduate economics research proposal assessment data (Australia, 2023 cohort), the study leveraged prior GPA, English at home, and earlier test scores (plus demographic controls) to predict final research proposal marks, finding that AI tool use had no statistically significant effect on the overall mark (coefficients near zero once ability controls were included). This indicates that permitting AI for essay-based assessment, as implemented in this course, may not change measured performance on the research proposal, though causality cannot be inferred due to non-random AI use and survey response bias.

main_findings.dataset_used: Undergraduate economics research proposal (Australia, 2023 cohort; essay-based assessment)
main_findings.target_variable: Individual marking criteria subscores (scaled out of 100)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regressions by criterion (no ML). Table 3 reports no statistically significant effects of Used AI on Presentation, Topic, Literature, Methods, or Implications; coefficients are small in magnitude across criteria.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using undergraduate economics research proposal assessment data (Australia, 2023 cohort), the study leveraged prior GPA, English at home, and earlier test scores to predict each marking-criterion subscore, finding that AI tool use showed no statistically significant effects on any criterion. This indicates that, under the study’s permitted-AI conditions and assessment design, AI use does not appear to selectively improve or harm specific components of essay-based performance, though the small sample limits power for detecting modest effects.

data.outcome_summary: This open-access case study examines AI tool adoption and its association with performance in an undergraduate economics research-proposal essay assessment in Australia (2023 cohort). The quantitative analysis uses a voluntary survey merged with administrative grading data for 69 students (two-thirds of respondents reported using AI). The main regression models predict the overall research-proposal mark (0–100) and five criterion subscores using “Used AI” plus ability controls (pre-semester GPA and earlier course test scores). The unconditional model shows a small, non-significant positive association (+5.391 marks), while models with ability controls estimate effects of less than 1 mark and report no significant AI effects on any criterion. The study also includes an intention-to-treat style cohort comparison (2023 vs 2022) and finds no evidence of performance gains. Limitations include non-random AI use, survey response bias (respondents were higher GPA), and no documented missing-data handling; moreover, the paper uses linear regression rather than ML algorithms.
